item.title: Verification of Statistical Properties: Redefining the Possible
item.description: arXiv:2611.26951v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We revisit the setting of Interactive Proof Systems for Distribution Testing, introduced by Chiesa and Gur (2018), showing that a simple twist on the task requirements may lead to dramatic improvements, allowing verifiers with constant sample complexity. We define and investigate the multi-prover and zero-knowledge versions of these interactive proof systems, using as flagship example the task of farness verification - the "dual" version of closeness testing. We hope our results will inspire others to investigate and analyze the power and limitations of multiple provers for distribution verification.
item.dc:creator: Cl\'ement Canonne, Sam Polgar, Aditya Vikram Singh, Aravind Thyagarajan, Qiping Yang

item.title: Hardness of algorithmic Kadison-Singer problem from approximate hypergraph colouring
item.description: arXiv:2611.27740v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In 2015, Marcus, Spielman and Srivastava published a solution of a strong form of a conjecture by Weaver implying a positive answer to the Kadison-Singer problem - an open question of interest to several fields of pure and applied mathematics. Specifically, they proved that for all $\alpha>0$ and finite lists of vectors whose Euclidean norm is at most $\sqrt\alpha$ and whose outer products sum to the identity matrix, there exists a signed sum of these outer products whose operator norm is at most $\sqrt{8\alpha}+2\alpha$. Since then, significant effort has been put into understanding the algorithmic side of the Kadison-Singer problem; that is, the task of actually finding a signing resulting in a matrix with operator norm at most $c\sqrt\alpha$ for some fixed constant $c$. The first hardness results for this problem were proven independently by Spielman and Zhang [APPROX'22] and by Jourdan, Macgregor and Sun [ISAAC'23]. In this short note, we prove that there exist values of $c$ arbitrarily close to $1$ such that it is NP-hard to distinguish indexed families of vectors for which there is a signed sum with operator norm equal to $0$ from those for which every signed sum has operator norm at least $c\sqrt\alpha$. This improves on the previous best bound by Spielman and Zhang. Our proof borrows significant ideas from the above mentioned hardness results, by adapting them to a reduction from the problem of approximating hypergraph colouring in the sense of promise constraint satisfaction problems.
item.dc:creator: Danny Vagnozzi

item.title: Pushdown Reachability Requires $N^{3/2}$ Time on Multitape Turing Machines
item.description: arXiv:2611.27814v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pushdown reachability, or equivalently, language non-emptiness of pushdown automata (PDA), is a fundamental problem in automata theory and program analysis. We show that, for every $\epsilon >0$, no deterministic multitape Turing machine can decide pushdown reachability in $O(N^{\frac{3}{2}-\epsilon})$ time, where $N$ is the input size. The lower bound already holds for \emph{sparse instances}, i.e., instances in which the number of transitions is linear in the number of states. This gives the first unconditional super-linear lower bound for pushdown reachability. Furthermore, we also extend this result and show that for any $\epsilon > 0$ and $k \ge 1$, no deterministic multitape Turing machine can decide the intersection non-emptiness problem of one PDA and $k-1$ NFAs in time $O(N^{\frac{3k}{2}-\epsilon})$, where $N$ is the input size. Finally, pushdown reachability is well-known to be quasi-linear time equivalent to many different problems in program analysis. Our result translates to all of those problems as well and provides the first unconditional super-linear lower bounds for those problems on multitape Turing machines.
item.dc:creator: A. R. Balasubramanian, Rupak Majumdar

item.title: Recognizing $k$-inducible Digraphs is NP-complete
item.description: arXiv:2611.27965v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A digraph is k-inducible if its arcs correspond to the pairwise majority relation of a preference profile with k voters. By McGarvey's theorem, every asymmetric digraph is k-inducible for some k, but for every fixed k there are digraphs that are not k-inducible. Whether a digraph is 1-inducible or 2-inducible can easily be decided in polynomial time. The complexity of deciding whether a digraph is k-inducible for every fixed $k\geq 3$ has been a long-standing open problem. We prove that deciding whether a tournament is 3-inducible is NP-complete and then leverage this result to show that deciding whether a digraph is k-inducible is NP-complete for every fixed $k\geq 3$. Our results imply that, unless P=NP, k-inducible digraphs cannot be characterized by finitely many forbidden induced subdigraphs.
item.dc:creator: Felix Brandt, Fabian Frank

item.title: No Polynomial-Time Algorithm For Tarski Fixed Points Unless Cryptographic Assumptions Fail
item.description: arXiv:2611.27977v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the time complexity of finding a Tarski fixed point. We provide a subexponential-time reduction from the Unique End of Potential Line (UEOPL) problem to the problem of finding a Tarski fixed point. Using a range of known cryptographic lower bounds for UEOPL, our reduction implies a range of conditional lower bounds on the running time of any algorithm that finds a Tarski fixed point. The strongest of these give quasi-polynomial-time lower bounds for the problem. We also obtain a similar quasi-polynomial-time lower bound for Tarski based instead on a weak exponential-time type hypothesis for UEOPL. These running time lower bounds match the recently discovered quasi-polynomial query lower bounds for the problem.
item.dc:creator: Eleni Batziou, John Fearnley, Alexandros Hollender, Rahul Savani

item.title: Computing Weighted Set Covers with Heterogeneous Stochastic Oracles: Deadline-Constrained Token Complexity
item.description: arXiv:2611.26656v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study computation in which a probabilistic Turing machine (PTM) uses AI systems, abstracted as heterogeneous stochastic oracles (HSOs), to solve Weighted Set Cover. A pilot study shows that an LLM can outperform weighted greedy. HSOs differ in capabilities, response distributions, latencies, and token costs. We study how the PTM selects HSOs to obtain, by a deadline and with a required success probability, a full cover satisfying a prescribed weight threshold, and we analyze expected token cost. For queries requesting full covers, assuming independent call successes and uninformative failures, we characterize by linear programming the minimum expected token cost for every feasible success probability. An optimal policy randomizes over at most two preselected sequences of oracle batches. Among policies attaining maximum success probability, the expected cost reduction of two-batch selection relative to querying all oracles in one batch is nonnegative and submodular. We construct an FPTAS for near-optimal cost reduction under heterogeneous response-time bounds. Computing an optimal two-batch selection is NP-hard but admits a pseudopolynomial algorithm for positive integral expected token costs. For partial-cover responses, the PTM combines returned sets across batches and turns. Once their union covers the universe, it verifies total weight directly or obtains a guarantee from LP-dual tests on retained partial covers. We give one-turn probability, token-cost, and hardness results and adaptive token-cost bounds under per-batch assumptions. A constructed instance shows that residual-guided querying can reduce expected token cost by a factor linear in the number of possible residual subproblems.
item.dc:creator: Jie Wang

item.title: Testability of Homomorphism Inadmissibility: Property Testing Meets Database Theory
item.description: arXiv:2611.26861v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this paper, we utilize the perspective of property testing to consider the testability of relational database queries. A primary motivation is the desire to avoid reading an entire database to decide a property thereof. We focus on conjunctive queries, which are the most basic and heavily studied database queries. Each conjunctive query can be represented as a relational structure $\mathbf{A}$ such that deciding if the conjunctive query is satisfied by a relational structure $\mathbf{B}$ is equivalent to deciding if there exists a homomorphism from $\mathbf{A}$ to $\mathbf{B}$. We phrase our results in terms of homomorphisms. Precisely, we study, for each relational structure $\mathbf{A}$, the testability of homomorphism inadmissibility from $\mathbf{A}$. We consider algorithms that have oracle access to an input relational structure $\mathbf{B}$ and that distinguish, with high probability, the case where there is no homomorphism from $\mathbf{A}$ to $\mathbf{B}$, from the case where one needs to remove a constant fraction of tuples from $\mathbf{B}$ in order to suppress all such homomorphisms. We provide a complete characterization of the structures $\mathbf{A}$ from which one can test homomorphism inadmissibility with one-sided error by making a constant number of queries to $\mathbf{B}$. Our characterization shows that homomorphism inadmissibility from $\mathbf{A}$ is constant-query testable with one-sided error if and only if the core of $\mathbf{A}$ is $\alpha$-acyclic. We also show that the injective version of the problem is constant-query testable with one-sided error if $\mathbf{A}$ is $\alpha$-acyclic; this result generalizes existing results for testing subgraph-freeness in the general graph model.
item.dc:creator: Hubie Chen, Yuichi Yoshida

item.title: Compiling Existential-Positive Queries to Bounded-Variable Fragments
item.description: arXiv:2611.26869v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A crucial property of bounded-variable fragments of first-order logic is that they can be evaluated in polynomial time. It is therefore a useful preprocessing step to rewrite, if possible, a first-order query to a logically equivalent one with a minimum number of variables. However, it may occur that reducing the number of variables causes an increase in formula size. We investigate this trade-off for the existential-positive fragment of first-order queries, where variable minimisation is decidable in general. In particular, we study the blow-up in the formula size when compiling existential-positive queries to the bounded variable fragment of positive first-order logic. While the increase of the formula size is always at most exponential, we identify situations (based on the signature and the number of variables) where only a polynomial blow-up is needed. In all other cases, we show that an exponential lower bound on the formula size of the compiled formula that matches the general upper bound. This exponential lower bound is unconditional, and is the first unconditional lower bound for formula size with respect to the studied compilation; it is proved via establishing a novel interface with circuit complexity which may be of future interest.
item.dc:creator: Christoph Berkholz, Hubie Chen

item.title: Parameterized Subset Sum for Integers and Solvable Permutation Groups
item.description: arXiv:2611.27244v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We show that parameterized subset sum for binary-encoded integers belongs to $\mathsf{W}[2]$, where the parameter is the number of selected integers. This improves a result of Buss and Islam, who proved membership in $\mathsf{W}[3]$. The proof uses an fpt-reduction to weighted CNF satisfiability without changing the parameter. For every fixed integer $d\geq1$, we also show that parameterized subset sum for permutation groups of derived length $d$ belongs to $\mathsf{W}[2d]$. The proof combines positive CNFs for addition in small abelian groups with an affine decomposition of a solvable permutation action. This gives circuits of weft at most $2d$ and depth depending only on $d$ for product evaluation. For every fixed nilpotency class, we obtain the stronger bound $\mathsf{W}[2]$ by an fpt-reduction to subset sum in abelian permutation groups. The reduction uses Hall's polynomial coordinates in a free nilpotent group and the Magnus embedding. For nilpotent permutation groups without a fixed class bound, we prove $\mathsf{W}[2]$-hardness, already for permutation $2$-groups.
item.dc:creator: Markus Lohrey

item.title: Decision trees for subword-closed languages over arbitrary finite alphabets
item.description: arXiv:2611.27454v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Moshkov classified binary subword-closed languages $L$ by the minimum depth of decision trees that recognize the words of length $n$ in $L$, or decide membership in $L$, using queries that return the $i$th letter of the input word. We extend this classification to alphabets with $k \ge 2$ letters. With the homogeneity and heterogeneity dimensions defined via pairs of different letters, the classification is the same as for $k = 2$: the deterministic recognition depth is bounded, logarithmic, or linear in $n$, the other three depths are bounded or linear, and there are five complexity classes. Since Moshkov's two-block structure lemma fails for $k \ge 3$, we prove a structure lemma with up to $k$ blocks. Our bounds are polynomial in $k$ and the two dimensions; in the bounded case they replace the exponential constant of the binary case by a linear one. We also show that the complexity class (one of the five) of a language given by a finite set of forbidden subwords can be computed in polynomial time. For several ternary languages we prove exact formulas for all four depths and check them by computation for small $n$.
item.dc:creator: Shahid Hussain

item.title: Cluster Editing in Subexponential Fixed-Parameter Time
item.description: arXiv:2611.27956v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Cluster Editing asks whether at most $k$ edge additions and deletions turn a given $n$-vertex graph into a disjoint union of cliques. For more than a decade, the fastest algorithm for it was the golden-ratio algorithm of B\"ocker with running time $O(1.62^k+n^{O(1)})$. Cao and Chen had conjectured that the subexponential running time $2^{o(k)}\cdot n^{O(1)}$ is possible, but this contradicts the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH). Recently, the breakthrough algorithms for 3-SAT of OpenAI and Anthropic refuted ETH itself. Our main result transfers running times from 3-SAT to Cluster Editing. If 3-SAT on formulas with $m$ clauses can be decided in time $T(m)$, then there is an algorithm that, given a graph with $n$ vertices and integers $k$ and $r$ with $2\le r\le k^{1/3}$, decides Cluster Editing in time $2^{O((k\log r)/r)}\cdot T(2^{O(r^2\log r)}\cdot k)\cdot n^{O(1)}$. Combined with the breakthrough algorithms for 3-SAT, this proves Cao and Chen's conjecture, as it solves Cluster Editing in time $2^{O(k\cdot(\log\log\log k)^{3/2}/\sqrt{\log\log k})}\cdot n^{O(1)}=2^{o(k)}\cdot n^{O(1)}$. The key ingredient is a sparsification theorem for Cluster Editing, the counterpart of the Sparsification Lemma for satisfiability: In time $2^{O((k\log r)/r)}\cdot n^{O(1)}$, it reduces a given instance to $2^{O((k\log r)/r)}$ weighted instances with $O(rk)$ vertices and degree $O(r)$, each of which is equivalent to a 3-SAT formula with $2^{O(r^2\log r)}\cdot k$ clauses. Conversely, by a known reduction with linear blow-up, every saving in the exponent for Cluster Editing is, up to constant factors, a saving for 3-SAT.
item.dc:creator: Alexander Firbas, Manuel Sorge

item.title: The Stochastic Arrival Problem
item.description: arXiv:2211.12982v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study a new modification of the Arrival problem, which allows for nodes that exhibit random as well as controlled behaviour, in addition to switching nodes. We study the computational complexity of these extensions, building on existing work on Reachability Switching Games. In particular, we show for versions of the arrival problem involving just switching and random nodes it is \PP{}-hard to decide if their value is greater than a half and we give a PSPACE decision algorithm.
item.dc:creator: Thomas Webster

item.title: Understanding Robust Catalytic Computing
item.description: arXiv:2605.09648v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Catalytic computing concerns space bounded computation which starts with a memory full of data that must be restored by the end of the computation. Lossy catalytic computing, defined by Gupta et al. (CoRR 2024) and fully characterized by Folkertsma et al. (Algorithmica 2026), is the study of allowing a small number of errors when resetting the catalytic tape at the end of a computation. Such a notion is useful when considering the robust use of catalytic techniques in the study of ordinary space-bounded algorithms. To that end, however, defining and characterizing less strict notions of error was left open by Folkertsma et al. (Algorithmica 2026) and other works (Mertz, BEATCS 2023). We expand the definition of possible resetting error in three natural ways: (1) randomized catalytic computation, which can completely destroy the catalytic tape with some probability over the randomness; (2) randomized catalytic computation, which makes a bounded number of errors in expectation over the randomness; (3) deterministic catalytic computation, which makes a bounded number of errors in expectation over the initial catalytic tape itself. We show a near complete characterization of the above models, both in the general case and in the logspace polynomial-time regime, by showing equivalences either between one another, to errorless catalytic space models, or to standard time or space complexity classes. Under a derandomization assumption, we show a near full collapse of all existing catalytic classes in the logspace regime
item.dc:creator: Michal Kouck\'y, Ian Mertz, Sasha Sami

item.title: Fine-Grained Hardness of Approximating Dynamic Time Warping
item.description: arXiv:2610.09233v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We prove conditional lower bounds for approximating dynamic time warping (DTW) over the uniform metric. Let $N,M$ be the lengths of the two strings and $n,m$ their numbers of runs. Under the Gap Block Disjointness Hypothesis, no deterministic algorithm $O(N^{\varepsilon})$-approximates DTW on two strings of length $N$ over three symbols in $\widetilde O(N^{2-\delta})$ time for any constants $\delta\in(0,1]$ and $\varepsilon\in[0,\delta/3)$. In particular, no deterministic constant-factor approximation runs in strongly subquadratic time. For run-length encoded strings with $n=m$, the Orthogonal Vectors Hypothesis rules out every constant-factor approximation in $\widetilde O((nm)^{1-\delta})$ time for every constant $\delta>0$. It also rules out $(N+M)^{1-\eta}$-approximation in this time for every constant $\eta\in(0,1)$. The bounds extend to every fixed metric with at least three points, including absolute distance on $\{0,1,2\}$. Both reductions use long runs to force equal-symbol matches on low-cost paths. For explicit strings, Boolean gadgets encode the source predicate. A deterministic disperser-based density amplification then yields the polynomial gap. For run-length encoded strings, we encode regular-expression membership so that the gap grows without adding runs.
item.dc:creator: Jihan Wang

item.title: Two $\operatorname{ReLU}$ Layers is All You Need
item.description: arXiv:2610.28587v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We prove that every $\operatorname{ReLU}$ network can be exactly simulated by a $\operatorname{ReLU}$ network with two hidden layers. We present two proofs: one that is based on fillings in homological algebra and a direct combinatorial proof.
item.dc:creator: Florestan Brunck, Christoph Hertrich, Kilian Ruess, Jack Stade, Amir Yehudayoff

item.title: Hypercube LSH for approximate near neighbors
item.description: arXiv:1702.05760v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A celebrated technique for finding near neighbors for the angular distance involves using a set of random hyperplanes to partition the space into hash regions [Charikar, STOC 2002]. Experiments later showed that using a set of orthogonal hyperplanes, thereby partitioning the space into the Voronoi regions induced by a hypercube, leads to even better results [Terasawa and Tanaka, WADS 2007]. However, no theoretical explanation for this improvement was ever given, and it remained unclear how the resulting hypercube hash method scales in high dimensions. In this work, we provide explicit asymptotics for the collision probabilities when using hypercubes to partition the space. Vectors at angle $\pi/3$ collide with probability $(\sqrt{3}/\pi)^{d + o(d)}$ in dimension $d$, compared to $(2/3)^d$ for random hyperplanes, and near-parallel vectors collide with similar asymptotic probabilities in both cases. The limiting exponential base tends continuously to zero as the angle approaches $\frac{\pi}{2}$ from below. For fixed near and far angular thresholds below $\pi/2$, these asymptotics determine the limiting LSH collision-probability ratio $\rho$. We further describe how to use hypercube LSH in practice. A direct partial-hypercube analysis gives a heuristic lattice-sieving time bound $2^{0.3347d+o(d)}$.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: 42nd International Symposium on Mathematical Foundations of Computer Science (MFCS 2017), pp. 7:1-7:20, 2017
item.dc:creator: Thijs Laarhoven

item.title: Revisiting the Graph Isomorphism Problem with Semidefinite Programming
item.description: arXiv:1908.06320v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: It is well-known that two graphs $G_1$ and $G_2$ on $n$ vertices are isomorphic if and only if their compatibility graph, an auxiliary graph on $n^2$ vertices, contains a clique of order $n$. In this paper, we give an exact conic formulation of this clique problem. We show that $G_1$ and $G_2$ are isomorphic if and only if a system of linear constraints over the cone of completely positive matrices is feasible. Since deciding membership in the completely positive cone is NP-hard, this formulation does not by itself yield an efficient algorithm. Relaxing complete positivity to positive semidefiniteness yields a semidefinite program whose infeasibility certifies that the two graphs are not isomorphic. We establish basic properties of this relaxation. Specifically, it is at least as strong as the necessary condition given by the Lov\'asz $\vartheta$ number of the complement of the compatibility graph, it never admits a strictly feasible solution, and it is implied by the degree-two level of the Lasserre hierarchy applied to a natural integer formulation of graph isomorphism. In light of known lower bounds for the Lasserre hierarchy, the latter indicates that the relaxation cannot decide isomorphism for all pairs of graphs. We leave open the question of characterizing the pairs of graphs for which the relaxation is tight.
item.dc:creator: Giannis Nikolentzos, Michalis Vazirgiannis

item.title: Precedence Constraint Scheduling on a Fixed Number of Machines
item.description: arXiv:2611.09392v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We give a deterministic exact algorithm for $P_m\mid\mathrm{prec},p_j=1\mid C_{\max}$ for every fixed $m\ge3$. The algorithm constructs an optimum schedule in $$ O(L)+m^{O(m^2)}\, n^{6m^2+13m+1} \, {\log n} $$ elementary RAM operations, where $n \ge 2$ is the number of jobs and $L$ is the binary input length. Its word size is $O(m^2 \log n)$ bits. A direct implementation on a deterministic Turing machine with a fixed number of tapes uses $O(L)+m^{O(m^2)} \, n^{6m^2+13m+1} \, \log^2 n$ steps. Thus both models have polynomial degree $94$ for three machines, apart from the displayed logarithmic factors.
item.dc:creator: Klaus Jansen
